title: DecisionV6
description: The record that an authorized actor accepted, refused or postponed a proposal against an exact state. A decision is the only thing that moves a proposal out of `Open`, and it is a permanent object rather than a status flip, because the question an audit asks is never `is this approved?` but `who approved it, holding what authority, against what, and when`. A DECISION BINDS `target_state_digest`, AND IF THE TARGET HAS MOVED THE DECISION IS REFUSED WITH `WI_DECISION_STALE`. The system does not re-attach the approval to the current state. That refusal looks unhelpful for about one minute and then saves a reviewer from having approved a figure they never saw: an approval that follows its subject around is not an approval, it is a subscription. This document is a DEFINITION LIBRARY: validate against a named member of `$defs`, never against the document root.

Decision.description: One decision by one actor. Both digests are required and neither is derivable from the other: `proposal_digest` says exactly what was read, and `target_state_digest` says what it was read against. A decision holding only the first would survive the proposal being edited after approval; holding only the second would survive the proposal being swapped for another about the same node.

proposal_digest.description: The exact proposal state that was decided on — text, rationale, delta and all. Pinned so that `they approved this` names a document nobody can revise afterwards. A proposal edited after a decision produces a new digest, and the decision then demonstrably describes something else.

target_state_digest.description: The state of the target at the moment of decision, which MUST equal the proposal's own target binding. Checked rather than copied: if the node has moved since the proposal was written, the decision is refused rather than recorded, because the reviewer's agreement was to a specific transition and the transition on offer is now a different one.

outcome.description: What was decided. A closed union rather than a string, because a decision surface that could record a free-text outcome would eventually record `approved with comments`, which is not a state the system can act on.

actor.description: Who decided. One actor per decision object: a quorum is several decisions, not one decision with several names, so that a later revocation of one signer's authority damages exactly their own decision and leaves the others standing.

authority_receipt.description: Proof that the actor held the capability at the moment of deciding, checked against an exact grant state. Carried on the decision rather than re-derived later, because re-deriving asks `does this actor have authority now?` and the question that matters is `did they have it then?` — and constraint C020 is what refuses a decision taken under a grant that had already been revoked.

reason.description: Why, in the actor's words. Optional for an acceptance, where the proposal's own rationale carries the argument. Policy SHOULD require it for a rejection and for every deferral: a proposer told only `rejected` has no way to produce a better proposal, and the next attempt will be a guess.

decided_at.description: When the decision was taken. Load-bearing rather than decorative here: authority validity, grant expiry and target currency are all evaluated AT THIS INSTANT, so a decision object that lost its timestamp could never be re-checked.

signature.description: Digest of the SignatureEnvelope over this decision, where policy requires a signed approval. Absent means the decision is recorded and unsigned, which is the ordinary case and must never be rendered as signed — an interface that showed a checkmark for both is the failure the field exists to prevent.

approval_state.description: Where this decision sits within a multi-actor approval rule, when one governs the target. Present so that a decision which is one of three required is legible as such, rather than appearing to settle a matter it has only advanced.

supersedes_decision.description: The decision this one replaces after a stale target forced a re-review. Retained so the record shows an approval taken twice against two states rather than one approval of uncertain vintage.

state_digest.description: Digest over the canonical decision state, so a release closure can bind the exact decision it relied on.

DecisionOutcome.description: What was decided. Modelled as a discriminated object rather than a bare enum because one outcome carries a payload: an acceptance conditional on a modification is only meaningful if it names the replacement, and an enum would have left that in a comment.

kind.description: The proposal as written was accepted.

oneOf.description: Accepted exactly as proposed. Says nothing about whether the change has committed; that is a transaction event, and the separation is the whole reason `Applied` is absent from the proposal status enum.

reopenable.description: Whether a reworked proposal on the same subject would be entertained. Recorded because `rejected, do not bring this back` and `rejected as written` are different answers, and a proposer who cannot tell them apart will either waste a week or abandon something that was wanted.

oneOf.description: Refused. The proposal is retained: a rejection is part of the record of how the current state came to survive.

until.description: When it should be looked at again, when a time is known. Absent means deferred pending something other than the calendar, which the reason should name.

pending.description: What it is waiting on — commonly another proposal or an obligation. Present so a deferral is a link in the graph rather than an item on somebody's private list.

oneOf.description: Postponed without refusal. A real decision that has been taken by a person with authority, which is why it is here and not a variety of `Open`.

replacement_proposal.description: The exact proposal state that WAS accepted. Required, because the original was not accepted and recording this outcome without naming what replaced it would leave a record claiming an approval of a proposal nobody approved.

oneOf.description: The proposal was not accepted; a modified one was, and this decision names it. Kept as its own outcome rather than as a rejection plus a fresh acceptance so that the modification is visibly connected to what it came from — a reviewer six months later needs to see that the accepted figure was the reviewer's, not the proposer's.

ApprovalState.description: How a decision stands against a multi-actor approval rule. Carried explicitly because the alternative is a surface that renders any decision as `Approved`, and a regulated release approved by one of three required reviewers would then look exactly like one approved by all three. The actual approval path must remain inspectable; no interface may reduce it to a badge.

rule.description: The rule in force, carried by value rather than by reference so the decision remains readable after the policy has moved on. A decision judged against a rule that has since changed must still be judgeable against the rule that governed it.

satisfied.description: Whether the rule is now satisfied. Derived from the recorded votes and the rule, never asserted: a field somebody could set would make the rule advisory.

votes.description: Every decision counted toward the rule, including the refusals. A rule tracking only assents cannot express a threshold that has become unreachable, and a queue that cannot say `this can no longer pass` will hold a proposal open forever.

outstanding.description: The roles still required. Named rather than counted, because `two more approvals needed` sends nobody anywhere and `awaiting legal_reviewer` sends somebody to legal.

sequence_position.description: How far a `Sequence` rule has advanced. Present only for sequenced approvals, where order is the substance of the rule: a legal review taken before the factual review it was supposed to rest on has not satisfied the sequence, however many signatures exist.

unreachable.description: Whether the rule can no longer be satisfied — a threshold with too many refusals left, or a sequenced role whose holder has none of the required capability. Recorded so a doomed approval fails visibly rather than by waiting.

ApprovalVote.description: One decision's contribution to an approval rule. A separate object because a vote and a decision are not the same thing: one decision may satisfy a rule for one target and count for nothing under another, and the role it counted UNDER is what makes it legible.

role.description: The role it counted under. An actor holding two eligible roles casts one vote under one of them, named here, so that a threshold cannot be met by one person appearing twice — which is the failure a rule expressed only in actor identities would permit.

counted_as.description: What it did to the rule.

at.description: When, which is what a sequenced rule is evaluated against.

VoteEffect.description: What one decision did to an approval rule. Four values, and the last two are why: a decision that was cast but did NOT count is a fact somebody needs, and a rule recording only assents and refusals would silently drop it.

oneOf.description: Counted against it. Under a threshold rule this can make the rule unreachable, which is a determinate outcome and better than an open queue.

Recorded and not counted, because the actor held no eligible role. Retained rather than discarded: somebody with an opinion and no standing has still been heard, and deleting the record makes the same objection arrive again next quarter.
Counted once and then displaced — most often because the actor decided again after the target moved. Kept so that the count is auditable rather than merely correct.
